title: Colossal's GenoMorph AI Hunts Dodo Genes From a Single Genome
excerpt: The de-extinction company built an AI platform that works with severely limited ancient DNA — and has already flagged some 2,300 editing targets for the dodo's skull and beak.
body:
• Colossal Biosciences has unveiled GenoMorph, an AI platform that identifies gene-editing targets for extinct species when only fragmentary DNA survives.
  • For the dodo, Colossal has just one genome to work from — against roughly 100 for the woolly mammoth — because tropical conditions degraded the bird's DNA.
  • GenoMorph has already flagged about 2,300 candidate DNA targets linked to the dodo's skull and beak, drawn from developmental data from chickens, quail, ducks and pigeons and skull measurements from more than 70 bird species.
  • The platform took more than a year to build and is designed to be reusable across de-extinction projects, not just the dodo.

Colossal Biosciences, the company trying to bring back the woolly mammoth and the dodo, has built an artificial intelligence platform to solve the problem at the heart of de-extinction: the DNA of extinct animals is scarce, fragmented and degraded. The platform, called GenoMorph, was announced on Wednesday and reported exclusively by TechCrunch.

One Genome Against a Hundred

The dodo illustrates the challenge. Colossal's scientists, led by chief science officer Beth Shapiro, have assembled one high-quality dodo genome. For the woolly mammoth, they have around a hundred. The difference is climate: mammoth DNA survived in cold, dry tundra, while the dodo's home — hot, wet Mauritius — destroyed its genetic record quickly. With a single genome, scientists cannot easily tell which genetic differences define the species and which are individual variation or damage.

"We don't have that luxury with ancient DNA from extinct species whose DNA is severely limited, and we can only get a small number of complete genomes."

— Ben Lamm, CEO and Co-founder, Colossal Biosciences

How GenoMorph Works

GenoMorph combines 3D morphology, comparative genomics and developmental biology to predict which genes shaped an extinct animal's form. To build it, Colossal collected developmental data from chickens, quail, ducks and pigeons, and combined it with genetic information and 3D skull measurements from more than 70 bird species. The system has already identified approximately 2,300 candidate DNA targets associated with the dodo's skull and facial features, including the bird's distinctive beak, which the company says can now move into laboratory testing. Lamm described the output as a prioritised map: the first edits the team believes will have the biggest impact on true dodo traits.

Part of a Wider Avian Push

The announcement came alongside a set of advances across Colossal's bird programme, according to Unite.AI's summary of the company's release: an improved dodo genome assembly built with technology from its dire wolf project, an expanded Nicobar pigeon colony — the dodo's closest living relative — the first hatched chicken embryonic stem-cell chimeras, and a lipid-nanoparticle system for delivering gene-editing tools into bird embryos. Founded by Lamm and geneticist George Church, Colossal describes itself as the first company to apply CRISPR technology to species de-extinction.

The Scepticism It Has to Answer

De-extinction remains contested science. Critics note that an edited pigeon carrying dodo traits would be a proxy, not a resurrected dodo, and that GenoMorph's predictions are only as good as their laboratory validation. The platform's real test is whether its 2,300 candidate targets produce the expected traits in living cells — work Colossal says is now beginning. If it works for the dodo, the same method could extend to other species whose DNA survived badly, which is most of them.
